title: Carbon cycle and climate change; Conservation and threats to biodiversity
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for Eduqas A-level Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: EV08a#t3 term and clue written for the game; EV08b#t1 term and clue written for the game; EV08a#t2 term and clue written for the game; EV08a#t1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: EC05c#N.2, EV08b#N.8, EC05c#N.16, EV08b#N.19.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Pollution
items.clue: Threat posed by pesticides and plastics

items.label: Keystone species
items.clue: An organism whose loss changes the whole community

items.label: Over-exploitation
items.clue: Threat from hunting, collecting and taking too many fish

items.label: Habitat loss
items.clue: Threat from deforestation, clearance for farming and drainage of wetlands

questions.stem: The bird species of a mountain in New Guinea were surveyed in 1965 and again in 2012. For most species both the upper and the lower limits of the altitudinal range had moved upslope, by about 100 m on average, over a period in which the region warmed. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: The species have expanded their ranges, since they now occupy about 100 m more of the mountain.
Because both limits moved equally, the species have lost none of their habitat area.
The correlation between warming and the shift proves that no other factor was involved.
The ranges of the species shifted upslope, tracking the rise in temperature.

questions.stem: A zoo has bred a rare antelope for 30 years from six founding animals. Which is the strongest scientific concern about releasing their descendants into the wild?

options.text: They are safe in the zoo, so release is not needed to secure the species.
Mutations will have given them alleles for zoo life, which they cannot lose again.
Being so numerous after 30 years, the herd must have regained the genetic diversity it started with.
Six founders carried few alleles, so the herd has little genetic variety to meet disease or change.

questions.explanation: Six founders carry few alleles, and inbreeding adds to the problem. Studbooks slow the loss, but cannot replace missing alleles.

questions.stem: A hypothetical small mammal lives only in cool meadows near the top of an isolated mountain. Over 40 years the region warms by 1.5 °C. Which outcome is most likely?

options.text: Its range expands, because warmer conditions open up more of the mountain to it.
Individuals change their genes to suit the warmer climate, so the species stays where it is.
It loses its lower slopes, and its range shrinks towards the summit.
It moves upslope with no loss, as the same band of temperature is still found higher up.

questions.explanation: The cool band shifts up, but a mountain narrows towards the top, so the area left shrinks. An isolated summit leaves nowhere cooler to go: local extinction is a real risk.

questions.stem: A rare orchid survives in one wild meadow. Its seeds are now stored in a seed bank, and plants grow in a botanic garden. The meadow is due to be ploughed. Orchid seeds need a particular soil fungus to germinate. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: The orchid is now secure, because its seeds and living plants are held safely ex situ.
The meadow should be fenced and left alone, as keeping people out is all that a reserve needs.
The meadow should still be protected and managed, as ex situ stocks cannot replace the habitat or its fungus.
Seed banks can store any plant's seeds for ever, so the orchid can be regrown wherever it is wanted.
